definition.text: The principle that a company should report both how sustainability issues affect its own finances and how the company itself affects society and the environment.

facts.text: The EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive uses a double materiality test, covering impacts on both the company and the public.
The Global Reporting Initiative's standards focus on impact materiality, while the European reporting standards focus on double materiality.
By contrast, the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board focuses on financially material issues that matter to investors.

title: Physical and transition risk

definition.text: The two kinds of climate risk: physical risks from climate impacts such as extreme weather, and transition risks from the costs of moving to a lower-carbon society.

facts.text: For the financial sector, physical risks mean damage to property, infrastructure and land; transition risks come from changes in policy, technology and consumer behaviour.
Physical risks of climate change top the list of business concerns for US and EU firms.
Transition risk includes the financial effects of carbon pricing and stranded assets.
In 2015 Bank of England governor Mark Carney warned that meeting the 2 °C limit could leave most fossil fuel reserves as stranded assets.

prerequisites: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures

title: Greenhouse Gas Protocol

definition.text: A set of standards that organizations use to measure and track their greenhouse gas emissions, the most common in greenhouse gas accounting.

facts.text: The World Resources Institute worked with companies to develop it, and its first version was published in September 2001.
It sorts an organization's emissions into Scope 1, 2 and 3; Scope 3 covers all other indirect emissions from its activities.
For most businesses the great majority of emissions are Scope 3, coming from the wider supply chain rather than the site or purchased energy.
Scope 3 was estimated at 75% of all emissions reported to the Carbon Disclosure Project, varying widely by sector.
Scope 3 is hard to report accurately: in 2022 about 30% of US companies reported it, and double counting is a concern.
The Science Based Targets initiative and the TCFD both cite it, and the ISO 14064 standard is based on it.

related: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures

definition.text: A company's voluntary practice of putting its own money value on its greenhouse gas emissions, alongside any carbon price set by government.

facts.text: It works like a Pigouvian tax inside the firm, making fossil fuel use more expensive.
As of 2024, 1,753 companies across 56 countries reported using it through the Carbon Disclosure Project.
The most common method is a proxy price built into investment decisions, used by roughly two-thirds of companies reporting to the CDP.
Some firms run an internal emissions trading system, where business units trade emission certificates.

title: Central banks and climate risk

definition.text: Green central banking: the idea that central banks should help reach net-zero targets and address climate change through their policies.

facts.text: By adjusting monetary policy and capital requirements, central banks can steer investment into green finance.
Bank of England governor Mark Carney backed the TCFD and called for financial firms to manage climate risk, notably through climate stress tests.
Many researchers argue that pursuing such goals raises serious questions about the legitimacy of independent central banks, which rarely have climate mandates.

related: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
contested_note: Researchers dispute whether independent central banks have the legitimacy to pursue climate goals.
